one_liner: Multi-tenant pub-sub broker on BookKeeper; vendor benchmark beats Kafka throughput, but the 100-partition win needs journaling off.
what_it_does: Apache Pulsar is a distributed pub-sub and queueing system. Stateless brokers serve clients, Apache BookKeeper bookies store the data, and a metadata store (ZooKeeper, Oxia, etcd or RocksDB) coordinates them. It has its own binary protocol and client libraries (Java in-repo; C++, Go, Python, Node and .NET in sibling repos), and offers both streaming and queue semantics (failover, shared and key-shared subscriptions, per-message and negative acks). It does not speak the Kafka protocol, so it is not a drop-in replacement for Kafka clients.
how_it_is_fast: Each topic is a managed ledger, a chain of BookKeeper ledgers written with quorum replication. The benchmark used ensemble 3, write quorum 3 and ack quorum 2, so a producer ack skips the slowest replica, while Kafka with acks=all waits on the in-sync replicas. Bookies interleave entries from many ledgers into sequential entry logs, index them in RocksDB (DbLedgerStorage) and keep their own write and read-ahead caches instead of relying on the OS page cache. The vendor credits these caches and separate disks for keeping catch-up reads from stalling producers. With journaling on, writes are group-committed to a journal on a dedicated disk. Producers batch by a max delay (1ms in the benchmark) rather than waiting on batch size.
when_to_use: Consumers regularly replay backlogs larger than RAM while producers keep writing, and publish latency must stay flat. In the vendor run Pulsar read at ~3.2GB/s vs Kafka's ~2.0GB/s, while Kafka producers' P99 rose to ~700ms.
Hot single partitions: in the same run one partition sustained 580MB/s (journaled) or 700MB/s (no journal) vs Kafka's 280MB/s.
Tail-latency-sensitive publishing at moderate load, where P99.9 and above matter more than P99. Kafka's P99.9 at 500MB/s was 54.56ms, and both Pulsar configs were lower.
Shared platforms that need multi-tenancy, quotas, auth, geo-replication and tiered offload of old ledgers to object storage in one system.
Applications that mix queue-style work distribution (shared/key-shared subscriptions, delayed delivery, DLQ) with ordered streaming.
when_not_to_use: You need fsync-before-ack durability and peak throughput at the same time. Default journaled Pulsar reached 800MB/s vs Kafka's 1087MB/s at 100 partitions, with higher P99 at 500MB/s (7.89 vs 3.46ms).
Small ops teams: a production cluster has three separately scaled tiers (brokers, bookies, metadata store), each needing JVM heap and direct-memory tuning. Standalone mode is for development.
You depend on the Kafka ecosystem (Kafka clients, Streams, Connect). Pulsar's protocol is different, and the open-source Kafka-on-Pulsar handler (streamnative/kop) is archived.

You want independent performance evidence. The 2022 result is vendor-run, and Confluent's 2020 OMB run on smaller i3en.2xlarge nodes found the reverse: Kafka 605MB/s vs Pulsar 305MB/s peak, and 5 vs 25ms P99, with Pulsar capped by a saturated journal disk.

integration.form: standalone multi-tier server (broker + BookKeeper bookies + metadata store) shipped as a tarball, Docker images and a Helm chart; the Java client is a published Maven module
integration.dependencies: Apache BookKeeper 4.18.1 (bookies run as their own service), a metadata store (ZooKeeper 3.9.5, Oxia, etcd or RocksDB), Netty 4.2, RocksDB 9.9 (bookie index), Jetty 12, protobuf/lightproto, Caffeine
integration.min_toolchain: Broker needs Java 21 on Pulsar 4.x; Java 25 is recommended for 5.0+. The Java client needs Java 17 or 21 from 4.1 (8/11/17/21 on 3.3-4.0). Building master needs JDK 21, 25 or 26 with the Gradle wrapper; bytecode targets Java 17.
integration.platforms: 64-bit Linux and macOS; Windows only through Docker; CPU architecture requirements not documented
integration.thread_safety: Client side (javadoc): PulsarClient is thread-safe and reusable, one Producer can be shared across threads, and all Consumer operations are thread-safe. Broker side: ARCHITECTURE.md says Pulsar has no clearly documented concurrency model.

gotchas: The 1600MB/s no-journal result uses OMB's bookkeeper-skip-journal.conf (journalWriteData=false, journalSyncData=false). That config also lists the two journal disks as ledger directories (4 instead of 2), so it gets more disk bandwidth as well as weaker durability.

Direct memory is the usual failure point. Bookie, broker and client 'OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory' reports recur (#19334 still open, #9721), and the Java client's default 64MB memoryLimit is documented as too low for high throughput.
Futures from sendAsync complete on the client's internal Netty I/O thread, so a slow callback on them stalls network processing for other producers (Producer javadoc).

Performance shifts between releases. The 4.0 shared-subscription rewrite (PIP-379) added ~15% end-to-end latency until the classic-implementation flags were set (#24490), and >200ms publish spikes in long 2.11 OMB runs are still open (#15792).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pulsar over Redpanda or AutoMQ when you want multi-tenancy, queue-style subscriptions and BookKeeper's quorum storage under Apache governance, and can move clients to Pulsar's API. Pick those two when existing Kafka clients must work unchanged. Pick it over Woodpecker (an embedded WAL whose own benchmark put Pulsar at 107MB/s) when you need a full broker with topics and subscriptions.
verified_claims_summary: StreamNative's 2022 OpenMessaging Benchmark (Pulsar 2.9.1 vs Kafka 3.0.0, 1KB messages, 3x i3en.6xlarge brokers with dual NVMe, 4x m5n.8xlarge clients, ZGC on both, Kafka RF3/min-ISR 2/acks=all vs Pulsar 3/3/2) measured no-journal Pulsar at 1600MB/s vs Kafka's 1087MB/s on 100 partitions (~1.47x), and 700 vs 280MB/s on one partition (~2.5x). Default journaled Pulsar lost the 100-partition test (800MB/s) and P99 at 500MB/s (7.89 vs 3.46ms), but won at P99.9 and above and on catch-up reads (~3.2 vs ~2.0GB/s).
status_note: Very active Apache-2.0 project: 4.2.4 and 4.0.13 shipped 2026-08-03 and 5.0.0-M2 on 2026-09-16. Active support for the 4.0 LTS ends 21 Oct 2026 (security fixes to Oct 2027), and Pulsar is deployed as a multi-service cluster, not vendored as a library.
